subject: paediatrics
title: Patent Ductus Arteriosus and Tetralogy of Fallot Anatomy

steps.tx: Persistent patency of the fetal arterial conduit diverts oxygenated blood from aorta into pulmonary circulation. In term neonates, functional closure of the ductus arteriosus occurs within twenty-four to forty-eight hours after birth as arterial oxygen tension rises and circulating prostaglandins fall. Persistent failure of closure constitutes **patent ductus arteriosus** (PDA), maintaining continuous aorto-pulmonary runoff throughout the entire cardiac cycle.
steps.say: Patent ductus arteriosus maintains persistent aorto-pulmonary blood flow after birth. Higher systemic pressure drives continuous runoff into the pulmonary artery throughout systole and diastole.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of patent ductus arteriosus connecting descending aorta to pulmonary trunk.
vis.caption: Patent ductus arteriosus connecting proximal descending aorta to the left pulmonary artery. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Continuous aortic runoff into low-resistance pulmonary vasculature widens the systemic pulse pressure. Because aortic pressure exceeds pulmonary arterial pressure during both ventricular systole and diastole, clinical examination reveals **bounding water-hammer peripheral pulses** and a widened systemic pulse pressure. Rapid run-off into the pulmonary bed during diastole drops the diastolic blood pressure, producing a hyperdynamic bounding apical impulse and palmar erythema.
steps.say: Aortic diastolic runoff into the lungs lowers diastolic pressure, creating wide pulse pressure and bounding pulses. Palpation reveals a hyperdynamic apical impulse.

steps.tx: Acoustic turbulence spanning both cardiac phases produces a pathognomonic thoracic murmur. Auscultation identifies the classic **continuous machinery Gibson murmur**, heard loudest in the left infraclavicular area and second left intercostal space. The murmur begins in early systole, crescendos to maximum intensity around the second heart sound (S2), and decrescendos through diastole without fading entirely before the next systolic beat.
steps.say: A continuous machinery murmur in the left infraclavicular area is pathognomonic for a patent ductus arteriosus. The murmur crescendos to peak at the second heart sound.

rows: Systolic thrill at lower sternal edge

steps.tx: Pharmacological cyclooxygenase inhibition promotes ductal smooth muscle constriction in premature infants. In preterm infants with significant left-to-right ductal shunting, medical closure utilizes **intravenous ibuprofen or indomethacin**, which inhibits cyclooxygenase enzymes to stop local prostaglandin E2 synthesis. If medical therapy fails or is contraindicated due to renal failure or active bleeding, surgical ligation or transcatheter coil occlusion is indicated.
steps.say: Cyclooxygenase inhibitors like ibuprofen or indomethacin close patent ductus arteriosus in premature babies by blocking prostaglandin synthesis. Surgical ligation is reserved for medical failure.

left.title: Pharmacological Therapy
points: Intravenous ibuprofen (10 mg/kg, then 5 mg/kg daily)
Monitor platelet count, renal function, urine output

right.title: Catheter and Surgical Closure
points: Transcatheter coil or Amplatzer duct occluder
Indicated in term infants and older children
Surgical clip ligation via left thoracotomy

steps.tx: Anterior and cephalad deviation of the infundibular septum produces four linked anatomical anomalies. The most common cyanotic congenital cardiac defect beyond the immediate newborn period is **tetralogy of Fallot**, accounting for ten percent of all congenital cardiac malformations. Embryologically, malalignment of the outlet septum creates four cardinal features: ventricular septal defect, right ventricular outflow obstruction, overriding aorta, and right ventricular hypertrophy.
steps.say: Tetralogy of Fallot is the most common cyanotic heart defect after the newborn period. Malalignment of the outlet septum creates a VSD, pulmonary stenosis, aortic override, and RV hypertrophy.

vis.alt: Anatomical diagram of Tetralogy of Fallot illustrating the four cardinal malformations.
vis.caption: Tetralogy of Fallot anatomy illustrating large subaortic VSD, infundibular stenosis, overriding aorta, and RV hypertrophy. [Credit: StewardMD]

steps.tx: Subpulmonary muscular narrowing dictates the clinical severity of cyanosis and right-to-left shunting. The primary hemodynamic determinant in tetralogy is the degree of **right ventricular outflow obstruction**, which is predominantly subvalvular infundibular muscular stenosis combined with valvular hypoplasia. Severe obstruction forces deoxygenated blood from the right ventricle right-to-left across the large non-restrictive VSD directly into the overriding aorta, producing cyanosis.
steps.say: The severity of subpulmonary infundibular stenosis determines cyanosis. When infundibular resistance exceeds systemic resistance, blood shunts right-to-left across the VSD into the aorta.

rows: Equalizes pressures in right and left ventricles
Aorta receives blood from both ventricles
Right axis deviation & tall R waves in V1

steps.tx: Auscultation in tetralogy reveals acoustic signs arising entirely from the stenotic pulmonary outflow tract. The characteristic physical sign is a **crescendo-decrescendo systolic ejection murmur** heard at the mid-to-upper left sternal border. Counterintuitively, the large subaortic VSD is auscultatorily silent because it is unrestrictive without a pressure gradient; the murmur arises entirely from turbulent flow across the stenotic right ventricular outflow tract.
steps.say: The systolic ejection murmur in tetralogy arises solely from the stenotic pulmonary outflow tract, not the VSD. When outflow obstruction worsens during a spell, the murmur softens or vanishes.

left.title: Mild RVOTO (Pink Tet)
points: Low resistance across pulmonary outflow tract
Child remains clinically pink without cyanosis

right.title: Severe RVOTO (Cyanotic Tet)
points: Profound central cyanosis and digital clubbing

steps.tx: Concentric right ventricular enlargement elevates the ventricular apex above the left diaphragmatic dome. Plain chest radiography demonstrates the classic **boot-shaped heart coeur en sabot**, characterized by an upturned apex secondary to right ventricular hypertrophy, a marked concavity in the mid-left cardiac contour from the hypoplastic pulmonary artery segment, and decreased pulmonary vascular markings producing oligemic lung fields.
steps.say: Chest radiography reveals a boot-shaped heart with an upturned apex and a pulmonary concavity. The lung fields appear dark and oligemic due to reduced pulmonary blood flow.

rows: Deep waist on upper left heart border
Absence of normal pulmonary artery curve
Hyperlucent dark lung fields, thin vessels
